text:
A: Hello? Oh, there you are. Sorry, I had the little picture of myself enormous and couldn't find you. Graham.
B: Hello, I'm Alison. Don't worry, it took me ages the first time too.
A: Where are you, Alison?
B: Chester-le-Street, near Durham. And you're Newark? Joanne said she'd had a solicitor called Graham. Sorry, I hope that's all right, we were just saying who we'd had.
A: Ha, no, that's fine. Hopefully she didn't say I was late, because I was. I'm always late.
B: She said you were lovely.
A: Oh, well, that's very kind. She was lovely herself. Proper down to earth. And I've had young Callum as well.
B: Oh, so have I. Erm, I found him a bit hard going at first, if I'm honest. But once he got on about his trainers he was fine. He told me fake ones smell of glue.
A: Did he! He told me he'll be earning more than his dad by twenty-five. I thought, well, good luck to you, son. I wasn't earning anything at twenty-five, I was doing articles in Lincoln and living on beans.
B: He reminded me of our Danny at that age. All front, but you could tell he's a nice lad underneath.
A: That's what I thought. I'd have given him a proper tea and he'd have perked right up.
B: That's what me mam always said. Feed them first, then talk to them.
A: Very wise. Er, so what about you? Are you working?
B: Not at the moment. I was in a school office for about twenty years. I left a couple of years ago. Erm, I keep saying I'll find something part-time, a surgery maybe. I don't know.
A: Well, a good school office is worth its weight in gold. My Linda was a primary teacher, and she always said the office ran the building and the head just thought he did.
B: Oh, that's nice of her. I don't know if it's true.
A: It's true of my firm, I can tell you. Janet, my secretary, if she left I'd be stood in the middle of the room not knowing what day it was. Which, to be fair, is most Mondays anyway.
B: I think I'd have liked working with you, then. I like being the one who knows where things are.
A: You'd have had your work cut out. My desk is mostly files. There's a calendar behind me, I've just noticed, and it's still on last month.
B: Oh, I didn't like to say.
A: Ha! Polite to a fault. Do you, er, are you a church person? I saw your little cross.
B: Erm, yes, Methodist. I go to the chapel most Sundays. I sing in the choir at Christmas, but only in the back, mind.
A: Oh, I'm C of E, parish church. I go because Linda goes, mostly, and because I like the people. I do the tombola at the fete every year, I've done it so long they don't ask anymore, they just give me the box.
B: That's like my lemon drizzle. Nobody asks, they just expect it.
A: Well, if it's good, it's good. I'm partial to a lemon drizzle.
B: Sundays are a bit funny for me now, actually. Me mam died three years ago and we always went round for dinner after chapel. Sorry, I don't know why I said that.
A: No, don't be sorry. It's the routine, isn't it. It's the routine you miss. I lost my brother ten years ago and I still sort of expect him to ring after the Forest match. Daft, really.
B: It's not daft at all.
